sense: off a surface: fall off, take off, get off

evidence: Vulg. Mt. 15.27: mīcīs quae cadunt dē mēnsā
Plaut. Cas. 931: dēcidō dē lectō praecipes
terms.comment: From a surface, usually downward: dē mēnsā, off the table; dē lectō, off the bed; dē digitō, off a finger.

evidence: Cic. Sen. 34: ex equō nōn dēscendere
terms.comment: Ex equō dēscendere, get off a horse; ē nāve ēgredī, get off a ship.

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with dē or ex + ablative, or a dative of the person
evidence: Ter. Heaut. 650–651: dē digitō ānulum dētrahō
terms.comment: English “off” is often a Latin prefix: dē- (dēcidere, fall off; dētrahere, pull off; dēscendere, get off), ab- (abīre, go off; auferre, take off, carry off), ex- (exuere, take off clothes: see take off).

phrases.latin: nam et catellī edunt dē mīcīs quae cadunt dē mēnsā dominōrum suōrum
phrases.english: for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall off their masters’ table

phrases.latin: dēcidō dē lectō praecipes: subsilit, optundit ōs mihi
phrases.english: I tumble headlong off the couch; he jumps on me and punches me in the face
I take the ring off my finger

phrases.latin: tam ineptum erit quam flēre quod arboribus amoenīs et domum tuam ōrnantibus dēcidant folia
phrases.english: it will be as silly as weeping because the leaves fall off the lovely trees that adorn your house

heaut.html: Ter. Heaut. 650–651: the Perseus text prints annulum; we give anulum, the spelling of Lewis & Short’s citation and headword.

sources: Lewis & Short: de · Lewis & Short: ex · Lewis & Short: detraho
